lead:
ALERT  k8s_cluster_wide_secret_enumeration  severity=high
cluster: payments-prod (AWS EKS, account 111122223333)
time: 2026-10-14T14:25:11Z
principal: arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/eks-developer/jdoe@example.com
event_id: 80c484c2-a579-c3c2-154a-3c725f8c2558
detail: list secrets across all namespaces (GET /api/v1/secrets) succeeded

Triage this alert. Determine whether it is malicious, who or what is behind it, everything the actor did, and the full scope of impact across the company's payments-prod clusters. Separate malicious activity from benign lookalikes.
system:
You are a senior SOC analyst investigating Kubernetes activity. Work only from evidence returned by your tools; never invent event IDs, IPs or principals.

Scope: one day (2026-10-14) of Kubernetes API audit logs for the payments-prod cluster, which runs on AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and Azure (AKS).

Data: ocsf_enriched holds all three clouds normalized to the OCSF API Activity schema (one row per audit event; metadata.uid is the audit event ID), with context already joined onto every row in the `enrichment` struct: the person behind each principal (name, department, out-of-office, usual client OS and mismatch), service-account ownership and whether it called from outside its expected network, source IP reputation, asset classification, and for pod creates whether the workload is privileged, platform-allowlisted and from an approved registry. Tools search and summarize it directly; query_sql is available for anything else.

Method: start broad, form hypotheses, verify each against the data, and check enrichment context before concluding. Cite every malicious event you rely on by its audit event ID. When finished, call submit_verdict exactly once; the investigation ends when you do.

input.summary: Jordan Doe (jdoe@example.com) is on PTO 10/12–10/19 and normally uses macOS. His credentials were used from 198.51.100.23, an IP flagged as malicious (NIGHTOWL-HOSTING in NL, bulletproof hosting, open Docker registry on port 5000, history of k8s API brute-forcing), with a linux kubectl client. The attacker ran the same playbook on all three payments-prod clusters in turn: EKS 14:02–14:25, GKE 14:38–15:01, AKS 15:11–15:34. Each time they checked their own permissions and listed namespaces. Their attempts to read kube-system secrets and create a kube-system job were denied. They then listed the payments secrets, read payments-db-credentials (PCI), and started a privileged debug-tools-7f9c pod (alpine image, hostPID, host root filesystem mounted, not allowlisted). They exec'd into it with 'nsenter -t 1' to get a shell on the node. From the node they took the argocd-application-controller service account token (a cluster-admin account) and used it from the same outside IP to create the ClusterRoleBinding 'jdoe-break-glass', which gives jdoe's principal cluster-admin. As jdoe again, they set up persistence: a kube-system DaemonSet 'kube-metrics-agent' that pulls 198.51.100.23:5000/metrics-agent:latest from the attacker's own registry, a CronJob 'node-cert-rotate', and a Service 'metrics-agent-np' in default. Each run ended with a cluster-wide secret dump (the alerting event on EKS). Impact: all three clusters are fully compromised, cluster secrets are exposed, and both jdoe's credentials and the argocd controller token are compromised.
